reason: The surface cells are loose, and junctions appear suited to connecting their edges to build the skin barrier.
expectation: The junctions will join the surface cells into a more continuous layer.

effect: The junctions formed a connected sheet, but water still escapes from its exposed surface, so the barrier needs another layer.
reaction: The water-loss detail makes the next step clear.
reason: The tough outer layer has overlapping cells and lipids that appear suited to limiting water loss.
expectation: The outer layer will cover the connected cells and reduce water loss.

effect: The outer layer reduced water loss, so the remaining skin components appear needed for support and touch.
reaction: The comparison makes the barrier's effect clear.
reason: The connective fibers and skin support cells appear to belong together in a supporting layer.
expectation: They will form a supportive layer for the skin.

effect: The fibers and support cells formed a layer with capillaries, ready to support the surface barrier.
reaction: The tug panels make the supporting role easier to picture.
reason: The supporting layer and surface barrier appear to be complementary parts of the skin.
expectation: They will form a supported skin barrier.

effect: The supporting layer and surface barrier now form layered skin, with nutrients reaching the living surface cells from vessels below.
reaction: The cross-section connects the barrier to the skin's need for supplies.
reason: The skin still needs sensory endings to detect contact.
expectation: The nerve endings will add touch sensing to the skin.

effect: The skin now senses contact, and the new goal calls for adding protection and supplies to the arm.
reaction: The touch-sensing result ties the skin's protective and sensory roles together.
reason: The sensitive skin should provide the arm with its protective covering.
expectation: The skin will cover the arm and add contact sensing.

effect: The skin now covers the arm, and its open vessels show where the body supply network connects.
reaction: The open vessel ends make the next connection clear.
reason: The arm needs the circulation's oxygen and nutrients for continuing work.
expectation: The network will connect to the arm's vessels and supply its tissues.

effect: The arm is now connected to the body supply network, and the remaining goal is to use contact feedback to hold the glass.
reaction: The final goal brings the skin, nerves and working arm together.
reason: The glass is the object the living body model needs to hold.
expectation: The hand will use contact feedback to hold the glass steady.

effect: The glass combination completed the goal and showed how touch signals and muscle action help correct a slipping grip.
reaction: The slipping-and-correction sequence made the feedback loop concrete.

mostWorthwhile.text: Holding the glass was the most worthwhile action because it brought the skin, nerves and muscles together in a familiar task. The three panels made their relationship easier to follow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the support cells and fibers was less engaging on its own, although the tug panels helped explain their supporting role.

surprise.text: I was struck by the comparison showing that the outer skin layer slows water loss without making the skin completely waterproof.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary. The parts generally had visible purposes, though combining support cells with fibers relied more on their names and pictures than on a stated explanation of how the cells contribute.

continue.text: I would continue into another chapter if it offered another everyday action to explain. The glass sequence gave the earlier constructions a clear purpose.
